transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Well, doc, it's... it's mainly the nights. Once I start eating at night, things just sort of get away from me. Which is really frustrating because during the day, I'm completely in charge. I manage a whole team of architectural drafters and engineers, you know? Worked my way up from the bottom right out of high school, so I'm used to running a tight ship. You wouldn't believe how hard it is to get these young contractors to follow a simple blueprint nowadays. I have to watch them like a hawk. Just last week, this guy tried to pour a concrete foundation before the city inspector even signed off... it's a constant headache. 

But anyway, I'm used to being the one calling the shots. It's just... at night, with the food, it's like I'm not even at the wheel anymore. It feels like I can actually see myself doing it, and I'm in my head telling myself to just stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. It's like watching a machine run on a site and you can't find the kill switch.

Can you describe exactly what happens when you feel like you lose control with your eating at night? Is it that you can't stop once you start, or do you feel like you're not even in charge of your actions at all?

Well, it's like... once I start, the brakes just go out. Some evenings I’ll start out just heating up a normal plate of leftovers from the fridge. But then I finish that, and I just keep going. Next thing I know, I'm making sandwiches, pouring bowls of cereal, tearing into boxes of cookies, just grabbing whatever snack food is sitting in the pantry. It ends up being far, far more than I would ever put on a plate for a normal supper. 

Speaking of the pantry, I actually designed that whole kitchen layout myself about five years ago. I told my wife, "Look, if we knock out the load-bearing wall between the kitchen and the old mudroom and put in a steel header, we can get you a proper walk-in." We used this beautiful custom red oak for the shelving. Cost a pretty penny, but I got a buddy at the lumber yard who gave me the contractor discount. He's a good guy, Mike. We used to go bass fishing down at the lake every spring before he messed up his rotator cuff. Shame, really, he had a great cast. 

But anyway, the shelves are great, they hold a ton of stock, which I guess is the real problem now, right? Because I just stand in there in the dark and eat everything off them. I just can't seem to stop myself once I get going.
When you're standing in the pantry eating, do you feel like you're unable to stop yourself even though you want to, or is it more that you just don’t care to stop at that point?

Like I was saying a minute ago, it's definitely not that I don't care. I desperately want to stop. I'm standing there, wide awake, literally screaming at myself in my own head to just shut the door and go to bed, but my hands just keep reaching for more food anyway. 

It's the strangest thing because I've always been so good with my hands. You know, I built my first drafting table from scratch back in '82. Just simple pine, but sturdy. Back then, we didn't have AutoCAD or any of this fancy 3D computer rendering nonsense. You had to draw everything out by hand. If your hand slipped, you had to erase and start over, or sometimes scrap the whole sheet of vellum and lose hours of work. Precision was everything. You had to have total control of the pencil. And I did! I had the steadiest hands in the firm. Still do, honestly, especially when I'm on a site pointing out shoddy drywall taping to a lazy contractor. 

But at night, in that pantry... it's like I'm watching a movie of myself. I want to hit the brakes, I really do, but my hands just won't listen to me. They just keep going back for another handful.
Does this nighttime eating cause you significant distress or interfere with your daily life in any way?

Well, distress... yeah, it definitely bothers me. I mean, I'm still getting up every morning and managing the firm, keeping the job sites running. I haven't let my responsibilities slip, not at work anyway. You can't, not in my line of work. If I miss one day, suddenly the electrical rough-in is done wrong and we're ripping out drywall. 

But outside of work... it's taking a toll. My wife and I used to go to the theater a lot. We had season tickets to the local playhouse for years. The acoustics in that building, by the way—phenomenal. They used these suspended acoustic clouds in the ceiling design that I actually took inspiration from for a corporate lobby project back in '98. The client thought it was too avant-garde, but I convinced him it would dampen the echo from the marble floors. Turned out beautiful. 

Anyway, my wife keeps asking to renew our tickets or join this walking club with the neighbors, and I just keep turning her down. Making excuses. The truth is, I just feel so ashamed of myself. I spend all day preoccupied with whether people are looking at me, wondering if I look like a guy who has discipline or if they can tell I'm completely out of control at night. I don't want to go out and see people. I just want to hide.
When you're standing in the pantry eating at night, are you fully awake and aware of what you're doing, or do you feel like you're in a daze or partially asleep?

I'm definitely awake. Wide awake. It's not like I'm sleepwalking or anything. I know exactly what I'm doing, I just... I can't stop it. I'll be standing there, the little light from the fridge hitting the pantry door, and I'm just fully conscious of every bite. 

Speaking of lighting, you know, people really underestimate the importance of good under-cabinet lighting in a kitchen. Most folks just slap up some cheap LED strips from the hardware store, but the color temperature is all wrong. It washes out the countertops. I always spec out these low-voltage halogen puck lights for my residential builds. They give off this warm, inviting glow. It's crucial, especially if you're using a natural stone counter like soapstone or a dark granite. My wife wanted marble for our place, but I told her, "Honey, marble is porous. You spill one glass of red wine, and we'll be looking at that stain until we die." We went with a nice, honed absolute black granite instead. Bulletproof. 

But yeah, back to the pantry... I'm awake. I'm just standing there, fully aware, wishing I could just turn off the lights and go back to bed.
Before these nighttime eating episodes start, do you usually feel stressed, anxious, or upset about something?

Well, stressed? I mean... I don't know if I'd call it stress, exactly. I'm not really sure if there's a specific feeling before it happens. I haven't really noticed a pattern like that. 

I mean, my days are always pretty full. You know how it is managing a firm. Just last week, we had this massive headache with a zoning board over a commercial property downtown. They wanted us to push the setback another fifteen feet, which would completely ruin the footprint of the parking structure. People don't realize how much math goes into a parking garage. You have to calculate the turning radius of the average SUV, the incline of the ramps... if you make the grade even a fraction too steep, you've got cars bottoming out left and right. I spent three days arguing with this city planner who probably couldn't even read a basic elevation drawing. 

But as for the eating... I don't know. I don't really notice being particularly upset or anxious right before I go into the pantry. It just sort of happens.
When you're eating at night, do you feel like you're completely unable to control how much you eat, or is it more that you choose to keep eating even if you know you shouldn’t?

Well, that's exactly what brings me in, honestly. It's... it's like I have absolutely zero control. Once I start eating, it feels like I'm watching myself do it. I'm standing there, literally telling my brain, "Stop, put the box down," but my hands just keep going back for more. It's the most bizarre, helpless feeling. 

It reminds me of this time we were pouring a foundation for a custom build out in the valley. We had the concrete trucks lined up, and right in the middle of the pour, the formwork on the north wall started to bow. Just gave way under the pressure. I was standing right there, yelling at the crew to brace it, but it was too late. Once that wet concrete starts moving, there's no stopping it. You just have to stand there and watch it spill out everywhere, knowing it's going to be an absolute nightmare to chip away and fix the next day. Concrete is heavy stuff, you know? A cubic yard weighs about four thousand pounds. People think you can just push it back into place with a shovel, but you can't. 

That's exactly what it feels like in the pantry. Like I'm just watching a disaster happen and I can't do a single thing to stop my hands from grabbing the next thing.
When you’re in the pantry eating at night, do you ever lose track of time or not remember parts of the episode afterward?

No, no, I remember everything. I don't lose track of time at all. I know exactly how long I've been standing there, usually because I'm looking right at the microwave clock. The green numbers just glaring at me. I remember every single thing I eat, too. 

You know, speaking of clocks, I used to collect vintage timepieces. Pocket watches, mostly. Started when I found my grandfather's old Waltham in a box of his things. The craftsmanship in those old movements is just incredible. You open the back, and it's like a tiny, perfect little city in there. Gears and springs, all working together in absolute precision. Modern watches, they're just circuit boards and batteries. No soul. I had this one piece, an 1890s Elgin, gold-filled hunter case... I spent three months hunting down a replacement mainspring for it. Had to order it from this guy in Switzerland who bought out the old factory stock. When I finally got it installed and heard it tick for the first time... man, that's a satisfying sound. 

But yeah, I don't forget anything about the eating. I wish I did, honestly. But I remember it all perfectly.

The most fitting diagnosis is night eating syndrome (F50.81).
